questions.question: A chord of length 24 lies in a circle of radius 13. Calculate the distance from the centre to the chord, naming the theorem that sets up the triangle and the classic error to avoid.
questions.expected_answer: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord, so the chord splits into two halves of 12. The radius of 13 to an endpoint of the chord is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose legs are the half-chord (12) and the distance d from the centre. Pythagoras: d² = 13² − 12² = 169 − 144 = 25, so d = 5. The classic error is using the full chord of 24 in the triangle instead of the half-chord of 12 — the perpendicular bisects the chord, so the triangle only ever contains half of it.

questions.question: State the theorem linking the angle at the centre to the angle at the circumference, apply it to a centre angle of 120° and to a reflex centre angle of 200°, and explain the arc discipline that prevents wrong halvings.
questions.expected_answer: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is twice the angle it subtends at any point on the circumference (same arc). Centre angle 120° gives circumference angles of 60° on that arc. A reflex centre angle of 200° stands on the major arc, so the circumference angle on that same major arc is 100°. The discipline: both angles must stand on the same arc, so shade the arc between the chord's endpoints that the angles actually open onto before halving — halving the wrong centre angle (the non-reflex one when the reflex one applies, or vice versa) is the standard error, not the arithmetic. The corollary: a diameter makes the centre angle a straight 180°, so the angle in a semicircle is 90°.

questions.question: O is the centre; A, B, C lie on the circle with angle AOB = 80° on the minor arc and C on the major arc. Find angle ACB and the base angles of triangle AOB, writing the solution as claim-plus-reason lines.
questions.expected_answer: Line 1: angle ACB = 40° — reason: angle at centre is twice angle at circumference (both on minor arc AB). Line 2: OA = OB — reason: radii of the same circle. Line 3: triangle AOB is isosceles, so the angles at A and B are equal — reason: base angles of isosceles triangle. Line 4: the base angles share 180° − 80° = 100°, so each is 50° — reason: angle sum of a triangle. Every line must carry its reason: a correct value without a reason earns nothing, because riders are marked as chains of justified claims.
